utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Could the witness please be brought in. Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer, for your efficient co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, with the downsizing, Mr. President, I need all the skill-set I can get. While we're waiting for the witness, I just wanted to update the Trial Chamber on the witness order. We have an illness among our witnesses, as you may have seen. That was Witness PW-29. So the lineup will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please pause a moment. There's a problem with the earphone again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please sit down. I hope very much that your earphone -- that you are receiving now a translation in the language. Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. The witness order will be PW-27, PW-26, PW-48, and then in place of PW-29, we'll have PW-47, whose witness number is number 114. And if we still have time left over, we've made arrangements to have Witness PW-38, who is Witness 105, available at least for his direct examination. I understand from the Defence that they may not be prepared to cross him today, but at least we could get his direct in, and we may be at the end of the day anyway. That's the lineup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm a little bit confused, Mr. Thayer, about one number you mentioned in line 23 of page 1. You mentioned PW-29. We don't have him on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He is the one who is ill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I thought that would be PW-41.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I beg your pardon, Your Honour, that's PW-41. You're exactly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, good afternoon again, and we continue your examination. Please be reminded that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. And Mr. Tolimir has some additional questions. Please, Mr. Tolimir, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I greet everybody present in the courtroom. I wish you all peace, God's peace, and I hope these proceedings will finish in keeping with God's will. I would like to welcome the witness. I'm sorry that he had to. Stay. However, I could not ask him questions that I should have, since he changed the course of his testimony in the course of the cross-examination. Can we please see P318, page 3 in Serbian and page 3 in English. This is the statement that this witness provided to the OTP of this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while we're waiting for the document, I have a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the statement that you provided to the OTP, did you have a chance to peruse it in the Popovic case? Thank you. And if that was the case, is it true that you did not want to make the same changes did you in paragraphs 6 and 7?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter does not hear the witness. Could the witness please be asked to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please repeat your answer, if you recall the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I did not change anything in my statement, at least nothing in the essence of the statement has been changed. The essence of the statement remains the same. What I said then still stands. The first mistake -- the first error that I corrected, I can't remember what page was that on, does not change anything in my statement. It was just a typo that I corrected. In other words, I do not agree that I have changed the statement at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you saying this for my benefit or for the benefit of somebody else?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, for your benefit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you answered the question and you kept on belabouring, let me put things one at a time. First of all, I asked for Exhibit P318, page 3 in Serbian, 2 in English. And while we're waiting for the document, let me ask you: You said in paragraph 6 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 6: "At that time, I knew that Generals Miletic, Gvero and Tolimir were top VRS commanders on the General Staff, but I did not know their functions." Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: How did you know that those generals were commanders, but you didn't know their functions at the same time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was public knowledge in the media. Those generals were mentioned. It was a notorious fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you still think the same?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, before we move on, was it important for your job whose conversations you were following in order to decide how important the information was? Was it important who was in what function?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because there were conversations that were not interesting for us, for our job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we come to the very thing for which we're here. Do you see the last part of paragraph 6 -- but we have completed that already, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But in paragraph 6, in the statement that we are looking at, there's something missing. Look at the last sentence: "I do not recall receiving orders to move their antennas. I did not have the know-how to do that." Did I read the sentence properly, and is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you mention antennas at all within the context of your interview with the OTP in paragraph 6, because nothing up to then concerned antennas?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any influence on the way the statement was worded, but what I stated, I stand by. What I meant was in the wording, there should be "their antennas," and that's referring to the antennas that my superiors mounted before I joined the service. I didn't mean the aggressor antennas, although it may be construed, from the way the statement was worded, that I had the aggressor's antennas in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please answer my questions? I'm asking you how come you mentioned antennas, since in paragraph 6 there was no reference to antennas, but to the generals? Did anybody ask you about the antennas?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about all sorts of things, ranging from the time when I joined the service, including our equipment and antennas, and I said that I didn't have the know-how to decide where the antennas would be mounted, how they would be turned, or whether they would be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I see very well what you stated, and I read that you stated: "I don't recall having received an order to move their antennas. I didn't have the know-how." I'm asking you again. Why are you referring to the antennas towards the end of paragraph 6 and nothing referred to the antennas before?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't the one who decided how the statement would be worded. I don't know why the antennas are mentioned in paragraph 6 and not in paragraph 7 or 8. That is not up to me. I was not the one who drafted this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you wanted to move the antennas, did you have to have your superior's order for that?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we were looking for directions, we had to have an order, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were the antennas property of the State Security Centre that you worked for or were they property of the army? Was there just one person who maintained the antennas and who was in charge of the antennas?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So how come you know that there should have been an order if you wanted to change the antennas?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't receive any orders to do that on my own. When my superior was there, we would be his assistants. We would assist him in his job, and somebody would be in charge of the equipment. And as far as the antennas are concerned, I'm telling you that I didn't have enough know-how to know where to mount them, how to turn them, and when to change them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer my question. Why would anybody issue an order to you to move the antennas if there was a person who was in charge of the antenna system? I'm asking you why would anybody issue an order to that? Did you state what it says here?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did not remember whether I had ever received such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But explain to the Trial Chamber. Why did you refer to the orders, antennas, and state things like that in paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because my superior was there when those things were done. An order would not have been indirect [as interpreted] from the base. He would have been there, and it would only be logical for him to go out and to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I did not receive my answer, why you mentioned the antennas in paragraph 6. Nothing you said before led to the antennas. But if you don't want to answer, I don't want to insist.

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you only interested in the fact that the antennas are mentioned in paragraph 6? Is that all you are interested in, why the antennas are mentioned in paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm interested in is another matter. I am asking you why the statement refers to the order to the antennas if nothing before that led to the antennas in the order, and why is that in paragraph 6. And you gave me your answer.

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I wasn't the one who wrote the statement. I don't know why this reference is in paragraph 6, and I keep on insisting on that, I keep on telling you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think the witness answered as best as he could, and you should not dwell on this any longer. I think you will receive always the same answer. I would like to put a question to the witness. If I remember correctly, you made some corrections at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. One correction was related to this sentence. I noted that you changed the word "their antennas" and "our antennas." Is that correct? Do I remember that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are correct, that was one of the changes to my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a technical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the VRS have any antennae at the northern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the northern site? As far as I know, no. The VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have another question. You said: "I wasn't the one who wrote the statement." Who did write the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement, as such, is based on what I said. But the part in the sixth paragraph, this could be part of the context of the seventh or the eighth paragraph, because in paragraph 6 we have generals followed by the antennae immediately, so it was probably carried from another paragraph. I don't know why it was put in paragraph 6, though. However, the words are mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who did collect your information into this statement? Who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the cover page it is stated who was present when I gave this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do I understand that correctly, that you gave all your information you could give to the investigators, and they put this information together and set up the statement which you signed? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether, save for your antenna, there were any other antennae at the facility?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the same location, but a small distance away there were army antennae, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what was the distance?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but a hundred or 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there any need for you to move their antennae, since you mentioned a commander here?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose antennae? What do you mean when you say "their antennae"? Which antennae do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You heard my question. You choose your own answers. Tell me whether there were any breaking and entries at the site where you were.

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did any UNPROFOR or NATO representatives have their antennae at the northern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it something you are certain of or do you only base that on your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fully certain of that. Someone would have had to have been there to maintain them, had there been any. I'm positive that none of those bodies had their antennae there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you whether there were any NATO or UNPROFOR antennae at the northern site. I don't care if you say yes or no, but please give me a positive answer.

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a positive no, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please re-read paragraph 7, if necessary, if you need to refresh your memory. Thank you. Please look at line 6 of paragraph 7. This is the sentence: "We would later transcribe the conversation onto teleprinter paper, then type their handwritten transcriptions into a laptop ..." In the English, we have "their handwritten transcription." Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the version in my own language, it is as it is. In Bosnian, it doesn't say "their."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you compare the written text and the recorded conversations, as you stated in para 7, lines 11 and 12?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will read it out, the sentence in line 11: "We tried to be 100 per cent certain that what they wrote down was correct." My question is this: Why did you say "what they wrote down was correct"? Did you copy somebody else's conversations or did you do the recording?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday we corrected this mistake. The Prosecutor explained it. It's one of the mistakes we corrected. It wasn't what they wrote, but what we wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you think it was a typographical error or did you say that?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a typographical error. I would not have said "their notes," because I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us this: In para 7, you changed all of the third-plural pronouns into "we"?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I stated what the corrections were to be made, but I wouldn't say it was in all of the cases you mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know who succeeded or who took over the UNPROFOR equipment that was at the northern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information to that effect, that there had been any equipment and that someone took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber, what operations did you undertake, without referring to paragraph 7? What activities did you undertake when you transcribed conversations? Because paragraph 7 describes the procedure you used when intercepting conversations. Can you explain that now?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean I need to start with the recording, itself, or the transfer onto a piece of paper and the typing in?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you personally type in anybody's conversations noted down into a laptop?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said so yesterday. I was a trained teleprinter operator and a cryptographer. Hence, I was good at typing into a computer, and this is why it was usually me who did that, especially when it was urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were the one typing into the laptop, what computer programme did you use, since you say you were trained?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What software, what programme I used? Well, Windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What was the particular programme you used to type out a text? I don't mean the system.

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a Co-Editor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you compare the written text and the conversations recorded, as you say in paragraph 7, lines 11 and 12 in the original statement, on the occasion of your first statement to the Prosecutor here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lost you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you compare the written text and the conversations recorded?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained this nicely, I think. We would record conversations on the UHER and write them down on a piece of paper. Then we would go back and listen to unclear portions, be it a single word, or parts of sentences, or even a syllable. In that case, I was assisted by my work-mate to decipher the word as best as possible. By doing so, we could cross things out on the piece of paper, a number of times if necessary, and we usually destroyed those papers afterwards. The final draft was then typed into a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you mention teleprinter paper in this statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To try and explain what kind of paper it was. It was not a note-book. It was plain paper that could easily be destroyed afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you're on the topic of destroying it, did you destroy your papers at the same location where the army did that or did you do it separately?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you share the same mess with the army members present there or did you have separate restaurants?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We took our meals together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you share the same logistical support or did you only use their facilities, their rooms, for lunch and dinner?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who brought the food, but we ate and prepared our food together. I don't know who provided the logistics, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the facility commander have any -- hold any sway over you in discipline matters?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were certain norms in place, in terms of conduct at the site, but that was the scope of his authority. He could not get involved in our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the facility commander initiate any disciplinary proceedings against you or any army members, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber whether, before having testified in the Popovic case, you had occasion to review your statement in a language you understand? And if so, why did you not point out the errors then?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked that yesterday. I said I did. I read it and signed it, but these were merely technical errors and I may have overlooked them then. On my arrival here, however, I managed to find them, and I insisted that they be changed. This was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did your unit exchange information it received by way of intercepts with any other users?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was something of military interest, then we handed over certain things to them, and vice versa, although there weren't many such occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there a third user from whom you received information?

utterances.speaker: PW-027 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. This concludes my examination-in-chief [as interpreted]. I would like to thank you for coming back the second day. I simply had to put certain questions to you for the sake of testimony in general. Your Honour, Mr. Presiding Judge, this concludes my examination. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. I think we have not reached the stage of the Defence case. Therefore, it was the cross-examination and not the examination-in-chief, as it was interpreted. Mr. Thayer, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your evidence. You are now free to return to your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague, and you are free to return now to your home. Thank you very much again, but please wait for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For your safety, the screens should be closed first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, the next witness will be PW-026; is that correct? And I think the next witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, could you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. As you are aware of, there are still protective measures in place for you. Your name will not be known outside this courtroom, and Mr. Thayer has some questions for you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have P348 on the screen, and that shouldn't be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, shortly you'll see a document appearing on your screen. When you were here last time, we did this the old-fashioned way with a piece of paper being shown to you, but today it's going to be on your screen. And I just ask you to confirm whether or not you see your name on the computer screen.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P348 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall providing a signed witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in February of 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And recently did you have an opportunity to read that witness statement again in your own language?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, I did have that opportunity, and I did read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you attest before this Trial Chamber that that witness statement fairly and accurately reflects what you said to the OTP during that interview in February of 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, I can attest to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during that interview, were you also shown a packet, a booklet of 23 intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in February of 2007, when you looked at that booklet of intercepts, were you able to determine whether or not you took part in intercepting, recording, transcribing, and/or transmitting those intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes and yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, with the Usher's assistance, I would just ask that this booklet of intercepts be handed to the witness. And once we've completed this next step, we'll proceed to the 92 ter litany for the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask you to take a couple of moments. I know it's been a week - I think we met last Monday - but if you could take a moment and just flip through that booklet, and tell the Trial Chamber whether or not you can confirm that those are the same intercepts which were shown to you in February of 2007 which you have identified yourself as participating in.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I can confirm that I participated in the recording and the reproduction of these conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I want to turn your attention to tab 4 of your booklet. This is P330, for the e-court. I just want to clarify one thing before we move a little bit. I referred to a packet of 23 intercepts. You said you recalled reviewing 23 intercepts, and our booklet contains 21 intercepts. If we look at tab 4, do you see a report numbered 538? Tab 4. The first report on the page is 537. It's dated 11 July 1995. And at the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Yes, yes, that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, within this report, can you tell the Trial Chamber approximately how many, if we could call them, sub-conversations there were in this report?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: There are three sub-conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And now those have been combined into one tab in this booklet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And last time around, what we did was each of those sub-conversations got a tab of its own. That's why we had 23 intercepts in your booklet last time around. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, turning back to your February 2007 witness statement, can you attest before this Trial Chamber that were you asked the same questions today that you were asked back then, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, my answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution tenders P326, the witness's witness statement, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: As well as the 21 intercepts in the booklet, P327 to P347.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received, and it should be noted that the Exhibit P330, in fact, contains three different intercepts. For the understanding of the statement given to the OTP, it should be noted, all these under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I would note, additionally, that just for the record, in the English version, and the English version only, of the witness's statement, there is a typo there at paragraph 10. There's a reference to 20 typewritten intercepts, and one can clearly see that they've been numbered 1 to 23, and that's just a simple typo in the English version. The original B/C/S version is correct. At this time, Your Honour, I would like to read the Rule 92 ter summary for this witness. The witness became a Ham Radio enthusiast in 1978 and competed in amateur radio competitions between 1978 and 1985. He has a B category Ham Radio certification. During the war, he served in a signals and communications unit of the State Security Services. In December 1994, he began working occasionally as an intercept operator at the northern site, and by the end of January 1995 he was working regular shifts there. The witness typically worked five-day, two-man shifts. The army also had personnel present at the northern site, but he does not know from which unit. His unit focused on certain frequencies and channels, and he became familiar at the time with the names and voices of various political and military personnel, including the accused. The witness described the procedure used when intercepting, taping, and transcribing VRS radio communications as follows: A receiver would monitor radio-relay 800 and was attached to a scanner. When a particular frequency or channel was detected, they would begin recording and listen to the conversation to determine if it was of interest, and if so, they would continue recording it with an attached UHER recorder. They would then write out the recorded conversation onto pieces of paper by hand, then type their handwritten transcript into a computer, encrypt the transcript and send it off. If the conversation were urgent, they would immediately remove the tape, place it on another tape machine, and begin transcribing. They would destroy the handwritten transcripts. The witness and his colleague took turns transcribing and typing, and sometimes would listen to a recording repeatedly until they were certain of what they were hearing. If they could not hear a word or portion of a recording, they would place dots. If they did not know the participants, they would so indicate with Xs and Ys. Sometimes he would consult with the army intercept operators as another set of ears. They would always look for confirmation of a participant's identity; for example, by the participant being identified either by himself or others, or by voice identification. They would not write down a participant's name if they were unsure, since they did not want to take the risk of misidentifying a participant. Sometimes the witness would include in his reports intercept data provided by the army intercept operators also working at the northern site. He believes the data was provided on a disk and would typically be added at the end of his report with a heading indicating that it was from the army. The witness reviewed 23 intercept print-outs and confirmed that he was either the recorder/transcriber or the typist/cryptographer for each. His code-name and that of his colleague appear at the bottom of each. The side-by-side pairing of code-names at the end of the print-outs was meant to indicate recorder/transcriber first and typist/cryptographer second. However, he cannot be 100 per cent sure that this order was correct on every print-out. In any event, they were familiar with each other's intercepts because they worked so closely and listened to each other's conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I just have a couple of questions for you to expand a little bit on what you said in your 2007 witness statement, and also to touch on some issues that were raised in the Popovic trial. If we look at tabs 2 and 3 of our booklets, and this is P328 and 329 in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are talking about reports number 535 and 536. For the purposes of the English translation, they are both included on the same page. So if we're following the English in the booklet, we can just stay with tab 2. In your language, sir, in the original document, report number 535 starts at the bottom and then goes over to the next page. I just want to first confirm that you're following me.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, I'm following. I can follow you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we look at these two intercepts, they indicate that they are between General Gvero and President Karadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But, in fact, only one of the participants could be heard by you at the time you took this intercept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So who could you hear in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: We could hear General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in neither of these two conversations, from what we can see here, does either speaker identify President Karadzic by his name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So can you please tell the Trial Chamber how it was that if you couldn't hear President Karadzic, you only hear General Gvero, and we don't have President Karadzic identified by his name here, how was it that you identified, in the heading of this conversation, that the two participants were President Karadzic and General Gvero? Could you just explain that for the Trial Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: It was like this: Before any of the conversations conducted by the high-ranking officers of the VRS, those conversations were preceded by the conversations of their subordinates. It happened only rarely or actually never that high-ranking officers either made calls or received calls. They had their subordinates who did that. We knew their names, we knew their voices. One of those subordinates was Rajko Banduka, who always picked up the telephone if -- and in this case we're talking about Gvero. If Gvero wanted to talk to somebody, it wasn't Gvero who dialed the number he wanted to call. He actually delegated his subordinate, who then called the person whom he was supposed to call. He greeted him and announced the caller. In other situations, if somebody called Mr. Gvero, the person who called asked for Mr. Gvero and then he would be put through. What I'm saying is that the conversations of high-ranking officers were preceded by short conversations between their subordinates. We did not record their names because we were not interested in their conversations. What we recorded were only important things. You have to know that there was a shortage of tapes. We had to be very mindful of that. So if we had recorded the conversations of the subordinates, it would take up a lot of space on the tapes. Then we also had to save energy. Sometimes it took as long as 10 minutes for the interlocutors to start talking. We saved energy by switching on [as interpreted] the tape-recorder while we were waiting for the high-ranking officers to pick up the telephone. There were, as I'm saying, short conversations preceding the ones that we were interested in and that we did record, and from those short conversations we learned who the interlocutors would be, once we started recording their conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I just want to clarify one thing that I see here on the transcript. I have recorded as your answer: "We saved energy by switching on the tape-recorder while we were waiting for the high-ranking officers to pick up the telephone." Is that what you meant to say or did you mean to say something else in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: It was like this: Our tape-recorder would be switched off. Its engine would be switched off. The tape-recorder was still on, but we would switch off its engine to save energy. This is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And you also mentioned in your answer that sometimes it would take 10 minutes for the talking between the two participants who interested you to begin. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber, in your experience -- give an example? What accounted sometimes for that 10-minute wait that you had before the conversation began?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: There was a short interruption in the interpretation. Could the interpreter please repeat the last portion of the interpreted text that was interrupted?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can just ask the question again. I believe that would be easier for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you referred to sometimes a 10-minute wait. What, in your experience, was the reason for the 10-minute wait? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Well, sometimes those persons who were requested were absent, were not in the room, or were otherwise engaged. In any case, they were absent, and then the person on hold would be told to keep on waiting, if it was urgent. If it wasn't urgent, if the call was not urgent, then that person who called would not be put on hold, but said to call back later.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at P345 for a moment, please. This is tab 19 of the booklets.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could scroll up just a little bit on the B/C/S, on the original version, please, just to catch the very -- I'm sorry, other direction. Scroll down. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I see you're using the booklet. Feel free to use the booklet, if that's easier for you. Do you see report number 988?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to ask you a couple questions about this intercept, in light of some of the things you've said in your statement and during your testimony in the last trial. We have here a conversation at 1002 hours, and the date of the conversation is 1 August 1995, if we look at the original report. And we can see, if we look at the beginning of the intercept, we have somebody you've identified as Stevo telling somebody named Jevtic: "Listen, Ljubisa Beara is going to call you. You know who he is." And the other guy says: "Who?" And Stevo says: "Beara." And then the other participant says: "No, I don't." And then Stevo explains: "The man up there, my boss." If we go further into the conversation - and we may need to go to the next page in e-court in the B/C/S only - there's a reference to a Rajko. Do you see that reference to a Rajko? You'll see a line, sir, where Stevo says: "Just a second. Rajko, if you're listening, put this man through to Beara."

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber what then happens after Stevo says: "Just a second. Rajko, if you're listening, put this man through to Beara"?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Stevo spoke to Rajko, and Rajko -- just bear with me. I need to check the frequency. 779, 13. Stevo spoke to Rajko, and Rajko put him through -- or, rather, Rajko put Jevtic through to Stevo. Rajko was the one who put Jevtic through to Stevo, and then -- again, could you please bear with me. And then Stevo spoke to him, because he probably assumed that he was listening to that conversation. It often happened that those people who announced them and put them through also listened in, and they knew it, because they had to be on top of things if those who were engaged in the conversation had to be put through to somebody else. I don't know if I provided a clear-enough explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And then in your experience monitoring these channels and frequencies, who is Rajko?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Since this is the frequency and the channel is 13, well, it was probably Rajko Banduka I specified a moment ago, because he usually answered or put people through on this channel and that frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so how does Beara get on the -- get involved in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: He got involved -- well, technically speaking, you know how people are put through. A connection is simply made to a certain extension from the switchboard that Jevtic called. Yes, Jevtic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And then we have -- we can see, on page 2 of the English and, I think, on the page that you're looking at, you've written down that Beara gets on the line and says: "Hello, good morning. Ljubo Beara speaking." And then Jevtic introduces himself and says: "Jevtic." Beara says: "Nice to hear you." And then we see some dots. And can you tell the Trial Chamber, what do those dots mean?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: These dots probably meant that the other person said something we couldn't understand. It sometimes happened that one of the interlocutors said something we could not make out. This could have been something simple. But in any case, the dots would mean that we did not understand his entire utterance. Someone would say something that you simply could not understand, and this is how we marked such portions which were not heard well enough and which we could not decipher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And then you've written down that you heard Beara say: "I'm a colonel. Listen, man, Stevo's told you what we want." My question to you, sir, is: How common was it, in your experience, for these participants, whether they're VRS officers or high-level politicians, to identify themselves, as they have here, by saying their full name and their position? We have Stevo saying Beara's his boss, and you have Beara introducing himself by name and identifying himself as a colonel. How common was that, in your experience?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: It happened whenever the interlocutors spoke to each other for the first time. Then they would introduce themselves in full, and sometimes they would revert to pseudonyms or codes, such as 01, which was for Mladic because he was the person number 1. Frequently, they mentioned their names. One of the reasons was probably -- for being so open, because -- well, I don't know what the exact number of phones was, but on channel 13, Rajko could be reached via Serbia. The area code was 011, which is Belgrade. As far as I recall, the number began with 5 followed by a 3, I think. I remember that clearly. That was probably the reason why they introduced themselves so openly. They presumed we were unable to listen in on that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Just a couple more questions before the break, and then I'll conclude my examination-in-chief, with apologies to the Trial Chamber for exceeding my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have P339 on e-court, please. This is tab 13 of the booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you want to turn to tab 13 in your booklet, sir, or look at the computer, it will be up there soon enough. While we're waiting for this to be called up: When you received, you said in your statement, a disk from the army operators at the northern site for you to include in your MUP reports, was the intercept information on that disk being provided by the army encrypted at that point or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: It was not encrypted. We received them unencrypted. We would then attach them to our reports and mark them as material having been received from the army, and then we encrypted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So let's look at what's on the screen. Do you see a document with "CSB-SDB Tuzla" at the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this should not be broadcast, please. And the date should be 17 July, first report, 652.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see it there, sir, on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we don't even need to look at the English translation for the question I have. We see here reports number 652, 653, 654, 655.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page in the original, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At the upper left-hand corner, we see -- at the end of the intercept that started on the prior page, we see some initials and numbers and a slash and then some initials and numbers. What are those, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: The two numbers, the two codes?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Without saying the numbers, themselves, can you just tell the Trial Chamber what they are, please?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: These were our codes, mine and my colleague's.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, right below that, we see a heading. What does that heading say, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: It says that it was received from a unit of the 2nd Corps. The abbreviation, itself, the "PEB," should be -- although I could be wrong, it should be Anti-Electronic Warfare, I think, at least. I'm not 100 per cent about the acronym, but in any case, the material following that came from that particular army unit or department.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we see here that this army material was given the report number 656. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was that a MUP report number or was that an army number?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: It was our number, MUP number.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we turn the page in the original, we can see that there's more than one intercept taken by the army that's included in this batch that was given report number 656, so my last question is: Was that the normal procedure, for a batch, as opposed to just a single army intercept, getting a MUP number?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, this was standard procedure. We assigned only one of our numbers, specifying that that particular document was sent under that number, although it could have contained several reproduced conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That concludes my examination-in-chief. And, again, I apologise for exceeding the estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Tolimir, would it be a convenient time to have the first break now, and after the break you can then commence your cross-examination? Okay. Then we will adjourn now, have our break, and resume 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We apologise for the delay. The Chamber was occupied with another matter, so now we are back. And, Mr. Tolimir, please put the questions to the witness for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to greet everyone in the courtroom yet again, including the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we speak the same language, after each of my questions I will say, "Thank you," to mark the end of it, and please pause before providing your answer for the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P326. It is the statement provided by this witness to the OTP on the 6th and 7th of February, 2007. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please switch on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since I see on the cover page that the witness signed the English version, I wanted to ask him whether he also received the Serbian version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I don't see any signatures in the Bosnian version. I don't know. I can't recall precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us where you provided this statement in February 2007. Was it here at the Tribunal or somewhere in the B and H Federation?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone get in touch with you before that, announcing that a statement will be taken from you at the Tribunal about these events?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, I had been contacted in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber who contacted you and what they told you?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I cannot recall any particular names. I don't remember any names, but I do know that I was in touch with Tribunal personnel. They introduced themselves, and they were accompanied by an interpreter. This is how we got in touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So Tribunal personnel. Did you consider any documents on that occasion which you had created during the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: You mean when we first met? No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you contacted individually on that occasion or was a whole group of you from your unit contacted at the same time?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: They got in touch with me at that time, and there were two other work-mates of mine at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. These two work-mates, were they from the State or the Military Security Service?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: They were my colleagues from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were any of your superiors present on that occasion or were there any superiors from the army present on that occasion when you were contacted by the Tribunal representatives in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: It was in the place I hail from and where I still reside. There were two of my colleagues with me, one of whom had been my immediate superior back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he also present at the Tribunal when you provided your statements? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you provided your statement at the Tribunal, were there any members of your unit or any military units present on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you provided that statement here, was it typed only in English and then read back to you in Serbian, and that is how you came to sign it, or did you receive a version in either English or Serbian to check whether it reflected what you had said?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, I received a Bosnian version, which I read. As for why it was signed in English, I cannot say right now. In any case, I did receive a Bosnian version, which I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you receive it at the occasion of giving the statement or was it typed out later in English and in Serbian by those who took the statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I received it after it was typed out in Bosnian. They gave it to me to peruse it. It's been three years, so I can't remember whether I received it right away or after a while. In any case, if you're asking me whether I signed it in the same period of time when I provided a statement, then the answer is, yes, this is when I was given that version to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there two people typing, one in Serbian and the other one in English, in the same room on the occasion of the taking of your statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I can't recall precisely such details. There were not two people. There were two people present, but they were not typing, so there were no typists for either of the languages. It was only typed out in one language, but I'm not sure in what language -- which language came first. I'm not sure what the sequence was, because, after all, it was not up to me to determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were only those people whom we can see on the cover page present? If you look on the bottom of the page on the screen, were only these two people present?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did anyone type your statement at that moment?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I think they took notes, and then later on it was typed out. I'm not certain of that. I think it was written by hand and then typed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you write this statement or was it written down by the two people who took your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Those two people did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the statement audio-recorded?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you ever audio-recorded by the people taking your statements to be used as your evidence before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you arrived here at the Tribunal, did you have any meetings or were you trained about the way statements are written at the Tribunal and about the way statements are provided at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you ever go abroad during the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you attend any training after the war about the job that you had been doing during the war and later?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: After the war? Are you asking me about after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will be more precise in my question. After 1996, when the war ended with the Dayton Accord, did you undergo any training abroad about electronic surveillance?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your statement, paragraph 3 on page 3, you stated --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 3, please. Thank you. Thank you. My legal advisor is correcting me. I should have asked for page 2, paragraph 3, whereas I'd asked for page 3, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, you say that you started working in the State Security Service in April 1992. Is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you think that that was your obligatory military service or was it you employed at the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: At that time, I was a member of the reserve force. In practical terms, I volunteered as a reserve officer of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. From when to when did you work at the State Security Service? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: From April 1992 until March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement -- in your statement, in paragraph 3, you say that from January 1995 you started working at northern site. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us when the intercept group of your service was set up in the northern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: It was set up -- it was set up immediately. Or, rather, when I arrived, immediately after that a group was set up to work as intercept operators, but not in that location. We were moved to that location later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether you know if anybody from your unit of the State Security had undergone training, in view of the fact that the State Security Services had not been engaged in those tasks before the war, only the military did that?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were members of your group trained by the military for the job that you later did? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: We were trained, if that could be called training. It was not classical training. We were simply introduced to new pieces of equipment. We were explained how certain pieces of equipment worked, and if that can be considered training, then we were trained, although those things didn't last long. However, since we were all familiar with radio equipment and we had been all Ham operators before that, we were not strangers to most of the equipment that we were supposed to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive from your superior or from your unit note-books for manual transcribing of the conversations you intercepted?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did army members receive -- were they issued with such note-books?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know how they operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a shop in the vicinity of that facility where you worked? How close was the nearest shop?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: At that time, there were virtually no shops. There were, actually, but the nearest shop, as far as I can remember, was some five or six kilometres away from the site where we worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the first -- the closest village to the northern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly whether it was, because you could approach our facility from two sides, so I really don't know which village was the closest to us, on which side. But I believe that there was another settlement closer to us, but it did not have a shop. The one that I mentioned before was on the other side, and there was a shop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you were on duty, could you go and visit that village that was five kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me whether your base, where your superiors sometimes went back and carried either papers or tapes, was that base close or was it far?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: The base was in the centre, in the central MUP office. In the town where I resided, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the base any closer or did everything have to be sent or did everything go to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: What base are you referring to? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I mean the base where you sent the data to.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: That base was at the MUP. Our base was the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Okay. Let's explain for the Trial Chamber that that base was in the city. Let's not mention any names.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And where was the military base with regard to the northern site? How far was it from you? Was it also in the city centre?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the military base was also in the same city, in the same centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the commander of the unit that shared your facility also based there in that base?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I really don't know how they were deployed. I don't know when any of them came and who they were. I was not aware of how long they stayed, who was billeted there. I did sometimes see them, but I didn't know anything about their shifts, how they were manned. I knew some people who were their commanders, but I don't know who was whose superior. I was not aware of all those details because we didn't share the same offices with them. We did share the facility, but we each occupied our own space, our own offices and our own rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the facility have a kitchen, and is that where you received your regular meals, or did the meals arrive from a base which was outside of the facility?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Well, there were different ways of food supply. For a while, there was a kitchen in the facility [Realtime transcript read in error "city"], and then because of the shortage of water, food was brought from another facility, military facility, which was a bit further, but I don't know which units were billeted there. So there was a kitchen there, and we would receive food from there. In any case, we received food regularly in different ways. There was no need for us to go anywhere in search for food, as it were. We were supplied with meals regularly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, Mr. President. I note in the English transcript, we -- at page 39, line 7, there's a word that appears. There appears to be some question of what the word was that the witness said. And I heard the translation. I don't want to become a witness, but if we could perhaps have the -- that portion read back to the witness, just so we have a clear English transcript. Again, I think he said what he said, but I'm not sure if the transcript accurately reflects what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The problem is that our numbering is disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can give you the -- yes. It's line 7, page 39. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, we don't have page 39 because something has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Then it's page 9, and it's the sentence -- there's a paragraph and answer that begins: "Well, there were different ways of food supply. For a while, there was a kitchen in the," and what's printed in the transcript is "city" followed by a caret, the symbol, and then "because of the shortage of water." So that's just the portion I'm referring to, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I remember very well that I heard "facility" instead of "city." Is that correct? Were you talking about facility instead of city?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter confirms that they used the word "facility."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was talking about the facility, not about a city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you sent the transcribed conversations to your base on floppy disks, or did you courier them to the base, or did you use any other means to send those transcribed conversations to the base?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: The way we delivered our documents to the base was via a modem, which means that we have a PC which was connected to a modem or, rather, to a telephone line that we had up there, and by that modem connection we sent data, coded data, that is, to our base. That was the way we operated. What you described as a possible way would have been extremely slow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether, in the course of one day, did you maintain communication with the city centre or was that connection or communication only periodical? How frequent were your communications, how frequent did you receive supplies?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: There was a telephone connection, and it was used as needed. In any case, we could communicate with the base. We also had the modem communication that I just described for the transfer of data. In case our telephone lines were down, and that did happen, we had a reserve possibility to use our radio communication, the so-called Paket Radio, by which a radio set is connected to a PC, and that's how you could send data to the base by means of Paket -- Radio Paket communication. And you could use that Radio Paket communication for other purposes as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us which computer programme you used to record intercepted conversations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: In order to type the text into the computer, we used Word.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? What did you use? I didn't understand you. Could you please repeat what you said? Your answer was what? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Data entry was done in Word. I can't remember which type of Word, but that Word programme came together with the operative system Windows 3.11.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And was that used in the entire unit or was it only used for your documents, the ones that you processed?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Could you please explain? What do you mean when you say "processing"? I'm talking about typing. We used Word as a typing machine, and the document was later processed, encrypted, and so on and so forth. What you asked me previously was about typing, and we used Word. We had another encryption programme for data processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You answered my question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P327 and P328 on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Those are numbers 1 and 2 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about the contents of these documents. You don't even have to look at them. I'm not interested in the contents at all. Do you see the conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here you have them on the screen. Do you see that only one participant appears in both conversations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber and to everybody else how come that whenever UNPROFOR officers are involved in conversations, only one participant appears and no UNPROFOR officers are ever heard? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just an objection to that question, Mr. President. I don't think that's a fair reflection of the evidence that the accused well knows is before the Trial Chamber. I understand that this witness is capable of answering the question, but that is not a fair characterisation of the testimony that has been before the Trial Chamber for the last couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please bear that in mind, Mr. Tolimir. If you put a statement to the witness, it should correctly reflect what the witness has said. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am displaying here the transcribed intercepts which this witness recorded and signed the transcriptions. If it is not the case, I'll drop my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, please carry on with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can remove -- we can remove this one, and let's display P336 and P326. I'm not interested in the contents. Again, I just want to have it displayed, please. We are still waiting for it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 581.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The number P326 is the OTP statement. Do you want to have that on the screen? Perhaps you misspoke.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P336 on the left-hand side, and P327 on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on the screen now. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something about P581 [as interpreted] on the left-hand side. We can see that the letters -- the letters with diacritics in the B/C/S are marked with double Cs or Zs. Is this how you marked them?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In P327, we see that, for example, instead of an S with a diacritic, there's only an S, and instead of a Z with a diacritic, there's only a Z. How do you explain this? What was the reason for it?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I will try to explain it as follows: On the keyboard -- well, this is a technical issue. The computer was not adapted to the Bosnian language. When you tried to type letters with diacritics, these are the letters that come out. It's a computer thing. When you press those keys, this is what you get. That is why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: Did you have two computers for typing, and did you have a typist?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: We did not have a typist. And for a while we did have two computers, and then later on we only had one. For a while, we even had a laptop and a desktop, and we used both. So we combined the two, we used both. It also depended on who did the typing. Some people used only Ss instead of the letters with diacritics, or double Ss. Something else also happened. I'm trying to refresh my memory. It also happened sometimes that the encryption programme we used did this in the following way: If you typed letters with diacritics, when encrypting those letters would be encrypted in a certain fashion. And when they would be restored back to the usual script, this is what would come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this mean that at encryption, the computer inserted one sign, and when encryption was being removed, another came out; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Well, it basically means that those letters in the Bosnian language came out that way after encryption and -- well, yes, this is it. Those letters simply came out that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see these two documents. Which computer programme did you use in these two documents? Was it the same programme in both? And if you can, tell us what type of computer was used for both of these.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: As for the programme for typing, as I said, it was Word.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In both cases? Sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, it was Word. And as for the computers, I think it were the 286 processor computers. I think even the laptop was with a 286 processor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness, for having testified. I thank you for coming over here and discussing these things with me. I wish you a safe journey back. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President, this concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Thayer, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President, if the Trial Chamber pleases, one question. And if we could have P326 displayed and not broadcast. This is the witness's OTP witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked a number of questions about the actual taking of your statement, and who typed what, and which version came first, the English version or the Bosnian version, which one you signed, and so forth. I just want to ask you a couple of questions perhaps to clarify that issue. Do you see your statement on the screen, both in your language and in the English language, the latter having your signature at the bottom? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. In the English version, if we could turn to page 5, please. And in the Bosnian version, that is page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need the English version. Both are in B/C/S now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've flipped them. On the left, we have the English version, and do you see where your signature is down at the very bottom of page 5?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in the corresponding Bosnian translation of that on the right-hand part of the screen, do you see where it says "Witness Acknowledgment" in your language? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what does -- if you would just read that witness acknowledgment out loud in your own language from that B/C/S version. What does that say there?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in? Please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. Is that better, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: This is fine, this is fine. The statement was read back to me in Bosnian language and contains everything I have said, according to my knowledge and recollection. I gave this statement voluntarily, and I'm aware that it may be used in a criminal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the crimes committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia after 1991, and that I may be summoned to publicly testify at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
