utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, in February of 2007, were you able to read English well enough to read a witness statement in English or did you have to have somebody read the witness statement back to you?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I could not read it in English. It was read back to me in Bosnian, and I understood it fully. I signed it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So when we see, in the English version, in the English language, the witness acknowledgment which you've signed, how was it at the time that you were able to sign your name there when you weren't able to read the English language, just to clarify the situation, I hope, once and for all?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: It is precisely as I said. The statement was read back to me, and I was acquainted with what was taken down as my words. This was the only way to do it, because I don't speak any English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So does this help you figure out which version came first, the English version or the Bosnian version? And I'm speaking about the written versions of your witness statement.

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: The statement was written in Bosnian, the one that was read back to me. Yes, in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If that's your recollection, can you tell the Trial Chamber why you signed the English version and not the Bosnian version?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I can't remember why. It's been three years. I really can't remember why I signed the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. But please help me to understand the last topic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who was it who read back to you your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: The interpreter who signed it. We could see it a moment ago. There was a name there in the English version. The interpreter who was there read back the statement to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was it a man or a woman?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: A woman. If necessary, I can tell you the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. I just wanted this identification, to have it from you. And could you say which -- the text she was reading back to you, in which language this piece of paper with the text was, in English or in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: As far as I recall, she kept notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us that you signed the English version. Who prepared the English version? Who typed it before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I don't know. It wasn't typed before me. As far as I recall, my statement was taken and -- well, whether the woman taking the statement also typed, that's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us who was present in addition to the interpreter, the name we saw on the first page of your witness statement. Was that a representative of the OTP, of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did he write this text which you signed?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I'm not clear about this. Could you please clarify? Do you mean whether he wrote it or typed it out? You see, I don't know such details. I know that the statement was taken, that the woman wrote it, but I don't know when it was typed out and by what technical means. That is something I don't know. I don't think it was done on the spot. And after it was read back to me, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did all that happen at the same day?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: I was there twice for extended periods of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you look at the screen, there are two dates, 6th and 7th of February, 2007. And were the same people present at these two days?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A representative of the OTP and the interpreter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-026
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are there any additional questions? You will be pleased, sir, to hear that this concludes your examination. Thank you very much that you were able to come to The Hague and assist us, and now you are free, of course, to return to your normal activities. Thank you very much again, and the Court Officer will help you to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, thank you very much, again, for your assistance. And the next witness, I suppose, is ready to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He is, Mr. President. And I'll wait until the witness exits, but I -- I think I can perhaps add one thing to the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and goodbye, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. President. If the Court desires, we can put an investigator on the stand to talk about the process, for example, that engendered the witness statement, for example, in this case. As an officer of the Court, there's no dispute that those present were myself and an interpreter. Typically, we try to keep the interpreters out of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I think it's not necessary to --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- explain it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just -- I didn't know whether things got more confused or less confused. I did my best with the witness, and it was what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir tried to clarify, you tried to clarify, and I tried to clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, all right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But I think we will have more occasions to deal with this and similar topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In that case, may I be excused for the rest of the proceedings today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer. And Mr. Vanderpuye is welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please stand for a moment. Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Please read aloud the affirmation on the card shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Vanderpuye, it's up to you to examine the witness, but I think we should clarify there's no face and voice distortion in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is face distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Only face distortion and a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon to you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Witness. I have really not that many questions for you today, Witness, but I'm going to ask you, nonetheless, to speak a little slowly and allow a pause between the question and answer so that the interpreters have time to interpret accurately what you say and what I say. The first thing I'd like to do is to show you P364. That should come up on the screen in a moment. And I'll just ask you, without telling us your name, to confirm if you are the person named on this document.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that. Witness, do you recall having testified in the case of Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic on 20 February 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was your testimony truthful at the time that you gave it?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review that testimony prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you read the testimony, or was it read back to you, or did you listen to it, if you could just tell us?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I listened to the audio-recording and went through the written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does the -- does the testimony that you gave at that time, on 20 February 2007, fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined here today and if you were asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, I would give the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Witness. Mr. President, I would like to tender that testimony. I think it's been pre-marked as P362 and P363, and also the pseudonym sheet, which is P364.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The pseudonym sheet, P364, will be marked. It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Vanderpuye, I was notified that you were -- that you don't intend to admit the Popovic transcript, but instead the OTP statement. Was that a mistake or wrong information?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yeah. I do intend to introduce the Popovic testimony. The OTP statement is an exhibit to that testimony. I can do it either which way. It's really -- it's really a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to admit the Popovic testimony, with the OTP statement as an exhibit to that testimony. So I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These will be received as separate exhibits, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I intend to tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If that is not the redacted version, but the version under seal, the confidential one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe it is not the redacted version. It is the version under seal, in terms of the OTP statement. Is that what you're referring to or the testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The testimony, I've offered the under seal version, and I believe the redacted version as well, both, 362 and 363, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The confidential version will be received under seal, the other not under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I apologise for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Before I go on, let me just ask you this, Witness: Did you have an opportunity to review your OTP witness statement of 18 February 2007, in addition to your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And having reviewed that statement, can you tell us, is that -- was it a truthful statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you to be asked the same questions as concerns that statement, would you give the same answers as is reflected in the statement today?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to that statement, Mr. President, I would tender it as a separate exhibit, not a 92 ter statement, but just as an exhibit. It is P349 for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As I already said, it will be -- it was a little bit premature. I've already stated that this OTP statement will be received as a separate exhibit under seal. I don't have the right page on the screen. There's an error in the numbering of the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay. May I proceed, nonetheless, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a brief summary I'd like to read into the record of the evidence that the witness provided in the Popovic case. First, I would note the witness, in his evidence, adopted the OTP witness statement of 18 February 2007, which provided, in substance, as follows. And I will need to go into closed session for a moment, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1993, the witness was assigned to the southern site of the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit as an intercept operator, which at that time went by a different name. Upon his assignment, the witness received instructions concerning the operation of the relevant equipment from his commanding officer and began processing intercepted communications, following an established procedure. This entailed taping intercepted communications, manually transcribing them into note-books, and submitting the handwritten transcriptions for typing and encryption. The witness was demobilised soon after the Dayton Peace Accords took effect. Per his testimony, the witness confirmed having obtained and transcribed 12 intercepts from July 1995 pursuant to his responsibilities and duties as an intercept operator. The work of the operators was monitored by their superiors, who provided note-books and collected them after transcriptions had been entered into them. Their superiors would also advise the operators as to the urgency of a given intercept. Although they were not given specific instructions about what letters to use to denote a given participant, for example, undetermined participants were usually indicated by X and Y. Operators would always note down the channel, time, and participants for each conversation. The witness noted that it was the operators' job to tape the conversations, listen back to them, and write down only what was recorded into the note-books. If necessary, they would pause, rewind, and listen to a given recording repeatedly in order to accomplish this. Mr. President, that concludes my 92 ter summary, and I have some questions to put to the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is I'd like to hand the witness a copy of this booklet of intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to ask you: Were you shown a packet of 19 intercepts from July 1995, prior to your testimony here today, similar to the one that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to examine the original note-books containing the intercepts contained in the package?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the packet of intercepts that you examined, and the one in front of you, can you tell us, were the handwritten intercepts that are contained in the packet written by you? Were they in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you write down the intercepts contained in the packet during the course and scope of your duties and responsibilities as an intercept operator?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you write down the intercepts that are listed and contained in that packet in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Generally speaking, after you made a handwritten transcript of a given conversation, were the note-book entries that you made typed up?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how long, approximately, after your note-book entries were written down were they typed up? Was it immediate, was it the same day, was it several days later? If you could just tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: If the intercepted conversations were urgent, if they were of particular interest and content, such conversations were sent on immediately and transcribed immediately. If a particular conversation was not urgent, it would be typed out and transcribed at the end of the day. The transcription was done by my superior and his colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to compare the 19 handwritten intercepts contained in the packet to typewritten transcripts?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you confirm that your handwritten transcriptions are reflected in the typewritten transcripts?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do, if you can, is just to look through this packet that I've handed you and see if it corresponds to the document that I showed you just the other day, so that you can tell the Trial Chamber whether what you have in front of you contains your handwritten intercepts. You should be able to find handwritten transcripts underneath every tab in the note-book, so just take a look at it, and let me know if you see a document in there that -- well, let me know if you recognise your handwriting for every tab.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes. Since I've already had an opportunity to review this material, I can confirm that all of it is mine. However, when it comes to the transcript of one of my intercepted conversations, since the transcript was not done in the original -- actually, the transcript is not the original. The number is 7. The frequency is 259.675, 1749 hours, and the participants were Toso and the other was an unknown person.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you referring to tab number 7?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll discuss that in just a little bit. So with respect to the remaining documents -- well, first of all, can you confirm that tab number 7 is in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the remaining documents in this packet, can you confirm that those are in your handwriting as well?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, and I know because I've already had an opportunity to review all these documents, so I'm sure that they are mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. With that, Mr. President, I would like to tender into evidence all of these documents. I understand that some of them have been -- they've all been pre-marked, so I would like to move them into evidence. I can provide you with the numbers. It's P350 through P361, and then P365 through P371.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They have all been admitted into evidence in the Popovic trial, together with the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The last series that I gave you, P365 through P371, are new documents. They were not admitted in the Popovic trial. But the first series from P350 to P361 were all admitted in Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The first series will be received because they are related to the Popovic transcript, P350 to P361. Do you intend to tender them under seal or is it not necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It is necessary because the print-outs contain the name of the location, and, indeed, I think some of the pages of the handwritten documents reflect the initials of other operators, and that might be an issue as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To clarify the situation, Madam Registrar will provide a list, a memorandum, for everybody. The handwritten transcripts will be public because they don't contain the name of the witness, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, they don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But as we agreed earlier, under the same number with A, B, C, we will have the transcript and the translation attached to that, but with the same number and under seal. The last series was not tendered with this witness in Popovic, but will be received in the same manner, as you have shown them to the witness and he has identified them as his handwritings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, what I wanted to ask you was: Do you have a present recollection of the facts and circumstances concerning these 19 intercepts generally?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Look here, a number of years have elapsed since I discharged those duties. I remember doing them. These are documents in my handwriting. And I worked even harder than I should because I wanted to stay in the job. I did not want to go back to the front-line from which I had joined the service. I don't know how this sounded, but that's how it was. And, furthermore, I remember one particular conversation. It sticks in my memory. I can still remember it, and I often think of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter -- I guess it's an exhibit number now. It's -- just a moment. P352 in e-court, please. A, please, the handwritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In which tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Mr. President. It's tab 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, what I'm showing you is an intercept that's in tab 3 of the booklet you have in front of you there, and it's dated 17 July 1995, at 950 hours. It refers to Pandurevic, and it talks about an estimate of about 5.000 people. And Pandurevic says: "There are hundreds of them dead. You can't kill them all, there's so many of them." Do you have any recollection of this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you remember about it?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I remember the way they mentioned roughly 5.000 people who were on the move, that they were falling like flies and still they were human beings. I called my colleagues. I wanted them to be present while I listened to that conversation, because I was really impressed. It was a very heavy moment, and I still remember that conversation to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I can observe from the handwritten document here is that there does not appear to be any letter or person attributed to the remarks that are made. In line 1, where it refers to "neutralising a lot of them yesterday" and "hammering away with artillery," there's no indication of X or Y, and I wondered if you could explain why that is.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I don't know who was the person talking. I don't remember. But since there is no designation, there is no first letter, that means that no names were mentioned during the conversation. It looked more like two people talking about what had happened earlier that day. That was the way we saw it. I don't know who those people were. In any case, they were well informed, they were on top of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if I could show you part B of this intercept. This is the printed-out version. Yes, 3031B, please. I'm sorry, it's 352, P352B. And you will see it on the left side of your screen, and here we have an indication of -- rather, a designation of the speaker there as X. I think that's the case with the note-book, except for the bad photocopy. But here you see X and only X speaking. Can you tell us what that means and why that's the case?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: This means that we could only hear that one participant. The other was not audible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that something that occurred with some regularity during the course of your work as an intercept operator or is that something very unusual, that only one participant can be heard, while another could not?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: This happened quite often. It occurred with some regularity. And when we heard both interlocutors, we noted that, and you will see it in my reports on intercepted conversation. I noted where there were several interlocutors who identified themselves during the conversation. They identified themselves by their names, and we put those names where they belonged. But if they didn't introduce themselves, they would be designated as persons X/Y, although there were some other symbols we used, but most commonly we used X/Y. And when they identified themselves, then they were designated by the first letter of their names, and they would become identified interlocutors whose names appeared at the beginning of the intercepted conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for that. I understand it is the break time, Mr. President, and this is a good place to stop. I do have a few more questions and documents I'd like to show the witness, though, before -- when we get back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We must have the second break now, and we will resume at quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Before we broke, Witness, you had mentioned that when individuals didn't introduce themselves, that X and Y were commonly used, but there were some other symbols that were also used. I wonder if you could just tell us, briefly, what those symbols were.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: X/Y, asterisk, question mark. As far as I can remember, those were the symbols. I don't know if there were any others. We had not received a very specific order as to how to mark unidentified persons, so we chose those symbols for those participants in the conversations who did not end up being identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you able or allowed to engage in any type of analysis or interpretation in order to arrive at the identity of a given participant in an intercepted conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it? I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, when somebody wasn't identified in a given conversation, were you, as an operator, permitted to look at the context of the conversation and the content of the conversation in order to try and figure out who that person might be, even though they are not otherwise identified? Were you allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: It happened very rarely. We didn't do it on our own. We did not attempt to guess the participant's name and put it down on paper if we were not absolutely sure. In that case, we would inform our commander and asked him to join us in listening and help us with the identification, especially if that particular conversation was a very important one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could show the witness, please, P359 for just a moment. And I'd like to show you P359A. Mr. President, that's tab 8 in the booklet. I'm mistaken, I'm sorry. It's tab 14 in the booklet. I think I have the right one, actually. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you look at the second entry in your note-book, and it reads: "Listen." First of all, you can see that the conversation begins with: "It's Tolimir, he's asking whether you'll be coming up -- you'll be coming here." And then in the second entry, it says: "I won't be coming. Tell Dinko to be on standby with the unit. They are not to move without my order." Do you remember reviewing this particular intercept, and in particular with respect to the reference to Dinko in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, I recall this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know who Dinko is or do you have an opinion as to who Dinko is?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to engage in any guess-work. I understood the word to be "Dinko," but it could have been "Vinko," and that's why the word is in brackets and there is a question mark next to it, and that's how it was transcribed, I suppose. I left it to my superiors to make the final judgement as to whether the word was "Dinko," "Vinko," or whether it was somebody else. I suppose that there was a lot of background noise when I listened to that part of the conversation, and the closest to what I heard would be "Dinko." And that's why the word is in brackets with a question mark next to the bracket.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you aware of any VRS officer at the time, that is, in July 1995, with the name of Vinko, with a V?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But you didn't write that down in this particular intercept because you couldn't determine whether you heard "Vinko" or "Dinko"; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That was a determination that you were not allowed to make, based upon what you were able to hear; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: When cases like this one happened, they happened mostly because of the background noise, and one letter can make a huge difference. So if things like that happened, then I would call my colleagues, and vice versa, they would call me if they had such a case, and then we tried to decipher the word or even whole sentences together. How should I -- how can I explain? How should I -- when something wasn't clear, we invested joint efforts. We listened and listened again, over and over again, to such portions of conversations and tried to make -- how shall I put it? We tried to decide what word sounded the closest to what the interlocutors uttered at that moment, and we would indicate that. The operators would indicate such places in their note-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you P371A. And while that's coming up, you said that operators would indicate in their note-books, in some fashion, where there was some difficulty in hearing or transcribing a given word of an intercepted conversation. How would they do that? How would it be indicated in the note-book? You've indicated in your case you used brackets. Was that something that was prevailing at the southern facility, where you were?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Well, the customary practice was to put "inaudible," "intelligible," "unclear," different words, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have now P371 in e-court, and I want to just draw your attention to it. It's at tab 7 of the booklet. And what I would like to do is draw your attention to the indication here. It looks like it's about four lines or so into your intercept, and the intercept reads: "Toso speaking. "Just a moment, Toso. "Hello, Toso?" And then it says: "I'm listening."

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: [In English] Please, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think his booklet has fallen apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can look on the screen. It's in e-court, so you can look on the screen, sir, and you can -- you should be able to see it. If you need us to blow it up, we can do that too. Plus I have another one. Sir, you can see this one, I suppose. All right. I think you've got it now in front of you. It's at 1749 is the time, 20th of July. And about four lines into the intercept, there's a portion of it where you've indicated "inaudible." That line reads: "The one down there rang me and asked one," and then it says "inaudible," "French. They need to go there. He is the deputy commander of the Sarajevo Sector." And what I'd like to do is -- first of all, does that accurately reflect what's in your note-book or in the note-book?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The person down there called me," "intelligible." The French were supposed to come, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to go to P371B. This is the print-out. And for the Court, I think you'll find that on the page just following the handwritten text. It's on the very last page of the tab in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in this print-out, you can see that that very same line reads as follows: "The one down there rang me and asked one," and then in brackets it says "(the name of a UN member unintelligible) they need to go there, he is the deputy commander of the Sarajevo Sector." And that you can see clearly is different than what you have in your note-book, which doesn't mention "the name of a UN member unintelligible" in it. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how this process would occur when a note-book is transcribed -- I should say taken in to be typed up or a given intercept is taken in to be typed up?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: It was my task to record intercepts, listen to them, and transcribe them. My unit commander worked on transcriptions as well, including another work-mate of mine. As far as I recall, when we listened to conversations in parts which were unintelligible, there were always several of us there to try to be as accurate as possible in terms of what was actually said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so was this the result of a process where you worked together with other members of the unit in order to arrive at what would be appropriate to put in the typewritten version of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I don't recall this, specifically, but it happened on occasion; not frequently, but it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know who this Toso that's referred to in this intercept is?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your experience as an intercept operator, did VRS officers use or go by nicknames?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was customary. They addressed each other with nicknames frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is the name Toso here a nickname, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: It probably is, because the person introducing himself says, It's Toso here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As a nickname, do you know which VRS officer that it belongs to or refers to?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Krstic's nickname was Krle; Pandurevic's was Pandur; Popovic's was Pop.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I take it, then, you don't know which VRS officer this nickname Toso refers to.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I heard the nickname several times, but I really can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could show you P360A, please. That's going to be at tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. This is another intercept. I think you have it up on the screen now. It's dated 25 July, and the time of it is 0709 hours. And in this intercept, we have a conversation where X is requesting an escort vehicle with three soldiers from one Lieutenant Matic. And you can see further down, directing Ljubo, who is a participant in this conversation, to find Colonel Golic. X tells Ljubo to check with Krstic. And in the middle of the screen, you will see it reads: "Okay, and where is this Golic?" And X says: "He should be somewhere with Krstic. Check with Pop ..." Can you tell us who the Pop is that's referred to in this intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Let me find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It will be on the second page in the B/C/S. It's an ERN ending 417 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Pop, Popovic, Colonel Popovic. That was his nickname. It was used frequently. They had no priests.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: "Pop" in B/C/S means "priest."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They simply had the nicknames Pop, Krle. Jevdjevic's nickname was Jevdjo, and there was another person I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned a Krle, and you can see "Krle" here also in the same sentence. In English, it reads: "Check with Pop, he knows where he is, and he's somewhere with Krle." Can you tell us who that refers to?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: You mean the person referred to in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. In your note-book, you've written down -- it says "Krleta," I think, and you can see it in the third entry on the page in front of you ending -- with the ERN ending 417. It's right above the word --

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. It's right above the word "Milicicen" [phoen]. Do you -- and who does that refer to? If you know.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Krstic. "Krle" was Krstic's nickname. It was used frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. A couple of more questions, and then we'll be finished. Now, when these handwritten transcripts were typed up, were they sent anywhere?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Note-books would be taken by my unit commander, and he would probably pass it on to his superiors, although I didn't inquire about that. This was no job of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know how this was done, whether this was done using a courier, or if it was done electronically, or some other means?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: You're asking me about the note-books?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm asking you how the typewritten -- typewritten transcripts of the note-book entries, what was done with them? That's what I'd like to know. Were they sent on someplace on else, were they stored in the site? If you know, it would be helpful if you could tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I apologise. I do not understand again. Do you mean the transcripts or the tapes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you took your note-book to the typist, what did the typist do with it?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: He would return the note-book to us so that we could work on. As I said, if the information concerned was very important, it would be typed out immediately, and we used other note-books to take our notes in the meantime. The colleagues who worked on transcriptions were there to assess whether a particular conversation was urgent or not. If it was urgent, they would type it up immediately. So they would return the same note-books to us until they were used up, and such full note-books would then be taken by the unit commander. And I don't know what he did with them later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What was done, in particular, with the typed material? When you say it was typed up, what happened to the material that was typed up? That's my question, if you know.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I have no idea. It was no job of mine to inquire. I didn't participate in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do have questions, by your leave, although I won't be able to finish in five minutes. Not even e-court documents could be put up in that short a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have a little bit more, 18 minutes left, and I think we should use this time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We stopped working yesterday at quarter to 7.00. That is why I thought it would be the same today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry. We were sitting in the morning. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it was the time before that. It's not important, in any case. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, while we're waiting for your statement, P394, I'd like to ask you something else. Sorry, it's P349. Witness, I will not mention your name, and we won't go into private session for the sake of time. Tell me this: Were you mobilised into the brigade referred to in your statement after 1992, and what tasks did you have in that brigade before becoming an intercept operator? It's page 2 in e-court, but I won't ask for it to be displayed because the name of the unit is mentioned, and we would need to go into private session for that, which would require time.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I was mobilised into the 121st Mountain Brigade in Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you can display every page, it will not be broadcast. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you mobilised into the unit referred to or did you volunteer?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you volunteer to be put on the intercept unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you volunteer to join the intercept unit?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I was mobilised into that unit. It was my military specialist [as interpreted]. I was a signalsman in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you also volunteer to be moved from the town where you resided to the location where you worked as the operator at the southern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, I will waste my time putting the same question time and again, so I'd rather stop. I asked him whether he volunteered to be moved from his town to the location where he worked, and I won't mention the name of his town because he's a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In case I wasn't sufficiently clear, I was mobilised into the 121st Mountain Brigade, Kladanj, and later on I was transferred to this -- well, I was mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you undergo any security or intelligence checks and training before being moved to the southern site, where you worked as the intercept operator?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: In terms of preparations, my unit commander showed me what and how to do things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive the note-books immediately, and did you use such note-books throughout the time you intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I don't remember. I remember we had note-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever have to buy your own note-books or did you always receive them from your unit commander?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Well, regarding that, we even brought note-books from home, because at that time we didn't even have paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you whether you bought them yourself or whether you brought them in.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Well, some people brought them from back home, and at a certain point in time note-books began arriving from our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How far was the closest shop to the location where you worked?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Twenty-five kilometres --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: -- more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you trade flour for note-books and take it all 25 kilometres away to the nearby settlement?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Well, I told you what I can recall. At first, we brought our own note-books so as to have something to write on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How much time did you require to transcribe -- or, rather, to make the handwritten notes in your note-books for a single conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Well, it all depended on the length of the conversation in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you send the note-books or did you send transcribed, typed-up conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: It was my job to write everything into a note-book, having recorded it first. Then I would have to listen to them and write them down. We would then hand over the note-books to our unit commander, who worked on transcription, and he would be better placed to clarify it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll ask him when he gets here. Did you personally burn the note-books or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the role of the unit commander in deciding what would be the closest or the most accurate version of a certain conversation? This is something you have just discussed with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Anything that was unclear required his presence and the presence of other colleagues. We all consulted each other, when we listened to the same conversation up to 20 times sometimes, and then it would be up to the unit commander to have a final say. That's all I can tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the unit commander make such calls based on his own assessment or based on something else?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: For the most part, calls were made jointly. The majority of colleagues would opt for a certain option.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you discuss amongst yourselves what the questions put by the Prosecutor here could be, since we only touched upon that?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss any particular questions. I wanted to cite an example of something I had said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor said that you were going to get to it later, and then you said that you can recollect that rather well. It's in the transcript. It had to do with the 5.000 people who set out to break through. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then you were interrupted by the Prosecutor, who said that you will eventually get to that.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked me whether there was a particular conversation that remains etched in my memory. During his examination-in-chief, I said there was a particular conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you mean he asked you that here, with all of us present, or during proofing?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: In proofing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I won't ask you about the contents of the conversations you commented upon. I only wanted to ask you this: Did you make the selection of the intercepts to be presented here, or was it done by your commander, or perhaps by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Please clarify. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you make the selection of the 19 intercepts in the booklet, or was it done by your commander, or perhaps by the Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were all these conversations in the same note-book or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think so, though. There were several note-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could it be that there were conversations in a note-book taken down by several people?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, in cases where we changed shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did this occur because it took a certain period of time to process all that material or was there another reason?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did several operators process the same conversation simply because it required a certain amount of time to process it due to a lengthy conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I didn't understand yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that there were conversations which were recorded by two people. One would start, the second would finish; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why was it done? Was it done because of the lengths of the shifts, and when the shifts ended, or because of the length of the conversation and how long it took to process one conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Look here, whatever I was in the middle of recording, I had to finish it, irrespective of whether my shift finished or not. And then my colleague would come and would continue recording and transcribing. And it all -- it did not really depend on how long the conversation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether you recognised the voices of the VRS officers?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: At the time, I recognised some of the modulations, I recognised some of their voices, but now I don't recall any of them. I could tell them apart by the modulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever asked by your commander or by the Prosecution to assign some of the voices to some persons although you were not sure?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: It was never requested from me. I don't know if it was ever requested from the squad commander, who transcribed the conversations. How -- what orders he received from his superiors, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked this because the Prosecution showed you a telegram where a person is mentioned, although he was not a participant in the conversation. For example, Toso was mentioned. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did anybody ask you to assign that part of the conversation to a person or did somebody request that from your commander?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: No, there was no pressure put on me. I just recorded things as I heard them. I did not try to guess who Toso was, did I?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you -- I don't know what you put. I did not record the conversation. I just read what the Prosecutor showed us here.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I recorded things as I heard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. You said here that you thought that you heard "Vinko" or "Dinko." You're still not sure what you heard, and is that why you recorded things the way you did?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. "Dinko," I believe that there was a lot of background noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question. In the vicinity of southern site, was there a commander by the name of Dinko? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: In our site, in our location?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the town closest to southern site, did you ever hear of an officer by the name of Dinko?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I don't remember. I haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever record a conversation that was relative to the place where you worked, which was southern site, and the units that surrounded it?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your note-books, did you ever record a conversation regarding the units or the activities of the military forces that threatened the facility where you worked, the southern site, or its immediate environment?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I don't remember. I really can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In 1995, did you record anything but the conversations involving the VRS that are illustrated by the 19 transcripts that we've seen here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I don't know, I haven't a clue. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you be able to say something based on the note-books that were given to you to recognise?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: In the material that you have in front of me and that I -- that you have in front of you and I have in front of me, that's just one part of the conversations that I recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recall any conversation involving two participants that you recorded and that did not concern Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Do I remember what? Conversations involving people, who?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recall any conversations that you recorded that did not concern Srebrenica in the course of 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I don't remember them, but there were a number of them. I don't remember any specific ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You don't remember the contents of any such conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-048
utterances.text: I am unemployed. I prayed to God for that war to be over. I tried to push everything behind me. I don't know if you can appreciate what I'm saying. So I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. God bless you. May God be with you on the way back home.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've finished my examination, Mr. President. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you for all the interpreters and everybody who has helped me in the course of my examination. Thank you very much for everybody's patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir, for your very effective and short cross-examination. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You will be pleased to hear that, unexpectedly, you are released now, and you may return to your normal activities. Thank you for your attendance here and your assistance you were able to give the Chamber and the parties. Thank you very much again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you, Your Honours. It has been my honour to be here and give my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court Officer will assist you when we rise. Please stay there for a moment. Thank you very much. We adjourn now and resume tomorrow at 2.15 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of June, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
